topic: Agent Design Patterns and Multi-Agent Systems
content: Supervisor patterns coordinate and delegate to specialist agents, while reflection patterns alternate generation with critique and revision. Single agents can suffer context and prompt bloat and error contamination; multi-agent systems can separate responsibilities but add coordination risks. Planner–Executor separates planning from execution, while Router dispatches requests to an appropriate specialized path. Multi-agent systems can fail through duplicated work, cascading errors, and runaway loops, so handoffs and global execution limits require explicit controls.
key_concepts: reflection uses generation followed by critique/revision
single agents can suffer context/prompt bloat
router dispatches requests to appropriate specialized path

source.section: Agent Design Patterns and Multi-Agent Systems

content: AI agents differ from simple chatbots and deterministic workflows because they can use an iterative reasoning/action/observation process to decide runtime actions and tools toward a goal. Agents are most justified when paths are dynamic, inputs vary substantially, or tasks are long-horizon. Deterministic workflows remain preferable for predictable, auditable, high-volume, low-variance processes. Autonomy should be treated as a spectrum; greater autonomy requires stronger guardrails, evaluation, observability, and recovery.
key_concepts: chatbot responds without autonomous execution routing
agent can decide next actions/tools at runtime
deterministic workflows suit predictable fixed processes
simpler workflows reduce cost/latency for high-volume low-variance tasks
higher autonomy increases risk and control requirements

content: Human-in-the-loop controls are important when agents can make consequential, customer-facing, irreversible, or low-confidence decisions. Approval checkpoints should be risk-based rather than applied to every output. High-confidence low-risk actions may proceed automatically, uncertain actions may require confirmation, and low-confidence or high-risk actions should stop or escalate. Review interfaces should expose enough evidence and task context for efficient decisions while avoiding reviewer fatigue.
key_concepts: human review reduces risk for consequential actions
review for low-confidence or sensitive outputs

content: MCP standardizes how AI applications connect to external tools, resources, and reusable prompts, reducing custom pairwise integration work. A2A addresses interoperability between agents rather than agent-to-tool connectivity. Interoperability expands attack surfaces, including malicious tool descriptions, injected tool output, over-scoped credentials, and unsafe writes; mitigations include vetting/version control, output handling, scoped short-lived credentials, and confirmation gates for destructive actions.
key_concepts: MCP standardizes connections between AI hosts and external capabilities
standard client/server interface reduces pairwise custom connectors
tool providers and clients implement the shared protocol

content: The Agent Development Lifecycle progresses from scoping through prototyping/building, evaluation, deployment, and continuous monitoring/improvement. The MINT principle recommends starting with the simplest system that works and requiring each added layer of intelligence, tools, memory, or multi-agent orchestration to justify its cost, latency, security, and maintenance overhead. Evaluation should detect whether agents make meaningful progress and trigger bounded stopping, replanning, or escalation when progress stalls.
key_concepts: each complexity layer must justify its overhead
simpler deterministic or RAG workflow may be sufficient

content: Task state is ephemeral and scoped to the current run, tracking progress and intermediate results. Memory persists beyond a task or session. Semantic memory captures stable facts or preferences, while episodic memory captures time-specific past events. Memory backends should match access patterns: summaries compress conversation, vector stores support semantic retrieval, and key-value stores support deterministic lookup. Good memory design is selective about what is written and retrieved and includes evaluation of memory usefulness.
key_concepts: memory persists beyond the current task/session
episodic memory stores time-specific past events
separate chat history from durable memory

content: Errors compound across long multi-step agent workflows, reducing end-to-end reliability. Cost controls include using smaller models for simple steps, caching, limiting retries and maximum steps, and avoiding unnecessary orchestration. Latency can be reduced by parallelizing independent calls, streaming, prefetching, and simplifying routing. Safe tool execution requires allowlists, strict input/schema validation, scoped permissions, risk-aware approval for writes, and sandboxing where appropriate.
key_concepts: per-step errors compound across multi-step tasks
longer task chains reduce end-to-end reliability
use smaller models for simple steps

content: Agent evaluation should distinguish the execution trajectory from the final outcome. A trajectory records messages, decisions, and tool calls; the outcome is the final environment or task state and is the strongest evidence that the goal was actually achieved. Reliability across repeated trials can be evaluated differently depending on whether at least one successful attempt is acceptable or consistent success is required. Complex multi-turn failures should first be localized using end-to-end task success and then debugged with step-level checks, simplified single-turn baselines, and controlled reintroduction of conversation context.
common_misconceptions: A successful-looking transcript proves the task succeeded
All valid agents must follow one exact reference trajectory

content: Production evaluation should measure both user-visible latency and economic efficiency. Time to First Token measures the delay before streaming output begins and strongly influences perceived responsiveness. Cost per successful task accounts for retries and failed runs rather than considering only one execution. Latency should be profiled stage by stage across retrieval, reranking, tools, model calls, and streaming. Cost controls include maximum-step limits, retry budgets, caching, and context summarization. Production monitoring should balance accurate evaluation with cost and latency by combining deterministic checks, sampled model-based evaluation, and human review for ambiguous or high-risk cases.
common_misconceptions: Cost of one run equals production cost per successful task
Every production trace requires an expensive LLM judge

content: Evaluation metrics should reflect the cost and type of application failure. Precision matters when false positives are expensive; recall matters when missing positives is costly. Exact word-overlap metrics can be poor proxies for open-ended semantic quality. Subjective qualities can be evaluated with explicit structured rubrics or focused binary checks. Generic metrics should not be trusted blindly when they do not represent application-specific goals, though they can help identify traces for error analysis. LLM judges should be calibrated against a human-scored gold set and disagreements should be analyzed before their scores are used for consequential decisions. Binary evaluation criteria can be easier to calibrate because they define a clearer decision boundary. Multi-level scales such as 1-to-5 or Likert ratings can be interpreted inconsistently unless each level has explicit anchors, increasing disagreement between human or model evaluators.
key_concepts: binary criteria provide clearer decision boundaries
multi-level or Likert ratings can be interpreted inconsistently
rating scales require explicit anchors for calibration
common_misconceptions: One generic helpfulness metric is sufficient for every application
Word overlap reliably measures all open-ended LLM quality

course_reference.section: Binary (Pass/Fail) vs. Likert Scales; judge calibration

coverage_enrichment.provenance_note: The local course export supports inconsistent Likert interpretation and focused binary checks. Clearer decision boundaries and explicit rating anchors are user-supplied calibration clarifications, not direct claims from the course export.

content: RAG evaluation separates retrieval quality from generation quality. Context recall asks whether the retrieved context contains the evidence needed to answer the query, while context precision asks whether retrieved context is relevant and useful rather than noisy. Faithfulness or groundedness checks whether generated claims are supported by retrieved evidence; response relevancy checks whether the response addresses the user's question. Abstention evaluation should include answerable and unanswerable cases. When retrieval metrics are strong but faithfulness is weak, diagnosis should focus on the generation stage and how the model uses supplied context.
common_misconceptions: A relevant answer is necessarily faithful
High retrieval quality guarantees faithful generation

content: One-hot vectors are sparse and do not naturally encode semantic similarity, while dense embeddings learn continuous vector representations where semantically related items can be closer. CBOW predicts a target word from surrounding context, while Skip-gram predicts surrounding context from a target. Static embeddings assign a fixed vector to a word regardless of context; Transformer representations are contextual and change according to surrounding tokens. Because self-attention alone does not inherently encode token order, Transformers incorporate positional information into token representations.
common_misconceptions: One-hot vectors capture semantic closeness
A static embedding changes with sentence context
Self-attention inherently knows token order without positional information

content: Tokenization converts raw text into smaller units such as words, subwords, or characters that can be mapped to numerical identifiers or representations for model processing. Boundary tokens can mark sequence beginnings and endings. Vocabulary size creates trade-offs: smaller vocabularies can fragment text into more tokens and lengthen sequences, while larger vocabularies increase parameter and memory requirements. Character-level tokenization can create very long sequences, while subword tokenization balances sequence length and vocabulary coverage. Sequential recurrent models process states step by step, whereas Transformer training can process token interactions much more in parallel.
common_misconceptions: Models process raw text directly without tokenization
A larger vocabulary is always better
Character tokenization is always more efficient

content: Self-attention uses Query, Key, and Value representations: queries express what information a token seeks, keys support matching against other tokens, and values carry information aggregated according to attention weights. Transformer encoders produce context-aware input representations, while decoders generate outputs autoregressively. Causal masking prevents a generative decoder from seeing future tokens during next-token training. Multi-head attention computes several attention projections in parallel so different relationships can be represented and then combined.
common_misconceptions: A decoder may freely attend to future target tokens during training
All attention heads necessarily learn the same relationship
Encoder and decoder have identical primary objectives

content: AI services should validate inputs before downstream execution and handle external failures explicitly. Network and model calls need timeouts and bounded failure handling so persistent errors do not create runaway work.
common_misconceptions: External API calls can be retried indefinitely

content: Python asyncio supports concurrent execution of coroutines and is well suited to I/O-bound network work. Independent calls can overlap waiting time. Concurrent tasks still require explicit exception, cancellation, timeout, and cleanup behavior; structured concurrency provides stronger guarantees for related tasks.
common_misconceptions: Async automatically speeds up CPU-bound work

content: Maintainable AI applications benefit from separation of concerns. API transport, orchestration logic, retrieval, model providers, evaluation, and persistence should have clear boundaries so components can be tested, replaced, configured, and evolved independently.
common_misconceptions: All AI logic should live in one API handler

content: AI services contain deterministic behavior that can be tested independently of model variability, including request validation, schemas, status codes, routing, transformations, and application rules. External dependencies can be isolated or replaced during tests. FastAPI supports synchronous and asynchronous API testing.
common_misconceptions: Every AI test must call a live LLM

content: Chunking balances retrieval precision with sufficient generation context. Large chunks may mix topics and reduce retrieval precision; very small chunks may omit necessary surrounding context. Overlap can reduce boundary information loss. Pre-chunking prepares chunks offline for fast retrieval, while query-time chunking provides flexibility at additional runtime cost. Semantic chunking uses semantic similarity or topic boundaries to keep related content together.
common_misconceptions: Bigger chunks are always better
More overlap is always better

content: Prompt engineering focuses on instructions and phrasing, while context engineering manages which information enters the limited model context and how it is structured. Long contexts can suffer lost-in-the-middle behavior and, over long interactions, repetition or instruction drift. Systems can mitigate this by filtering, reranking, summarizing, compressing, prioritizing relevant context, and storing state outside the prompt when appropriate.
common_misconceptions: A larger context window removes the need for context selection
Prompt wording alone solves context-management problems

content: Embeddings represent text as numerical vectors in a learned space where semantically similar text should be closer. Retrieval compares query and document embeddings using similarity or distance measures such as cosine similarity or Euclidean distance. Query and indexed document embeddings must be compatible; changing the embedding model without rebuilding the index can severely degrade retrieval and generally requires re-embedding the corpus. Cosine similarity compares the direction or angle between vectors and is less affected by vector magnitude. Euclidean distance measures the straight-line distance between vectors and is sensitive to both direction and magnitude.
key_concepts: Euclidean distance measures straight-line vector distance
Euclidean distance is affected by vector magnitude
common_misconceptions: Embeddings store the original text verbatim
Any embedding model can query an index produced by another model

course_reference.section: Embeddings: comparison of Euclidean distance and cosine similarity

coverage_enrichment.provenance_note: The added direction, distance, and magnitude distinctions are supported by the local grounded answer/grading guide.

content: RAG evaluation should separate retrieval quality from generation quality so failures can be localized. Retrieval metrics include Recall@k, MRR, and MAP. Grounded evaluation datasets can be created from trusted source contexts by generating question-answer pairs and filtering them for groundedness, relevance, and stand-alone quality. LLM-as-a-judge evaluation should provide supporting evidence, explicit scoring criteria, and structured evidence-based outputs to improve consistency. Recall@k measures how much of the relevant information is retrieved within the top-k results. MRR emphasizes how early the first relevant result appears by using its reciprocal rank. MAP evaluates ranking quality when multiple relevant results may exist by averaging precision at relevant-result positions. For synthetic RAG evaluation data, groundedness checks whether an example is supported by the source context, relevance checks whether it is useful and pertinent to the intended task, and stand-alone quality checks whether the question can be understood without hidden context.
key_concepts: Recall@k measures relevant items retrieved within top-k
MRR emphasizes the rank of the first relevant result
MAP evaluates ranking when multiple relevant items exist
common_misconceptions: End-to-end correctness alone identifies the failing component
An LLM judge needs no rubric or evidence

course_reference.section: RAG Evaluation: Basic Q2 and Intermediate Q2

coverage_enrichment.provenance_note: The local grading guides support the metric roles and all three synthetic-data checks. Explicit reciprocal-rank wording is a user-supplied clarification of the MRR description.

content: RAG retrieves relevant information from external knowledge sources and augments the model input before generation. This separates frequently changing factual knowledge from model weights. Fine-tuning modifies model behavior or parameters and is generally more suitable for behavior/style adaptation than frequent factual updates. Very large long-context prompts can increase cost and latency and introduce irrelevant context or lost-in-the-middle effects. Retrieval helps ground generation in selected external evidence. LLM generation is probabilistic: the model predicts likely next tokens rather than retrieving verified facts from a database. As a result, fluent output can contain unsupported or incorrect information. Retrieval can reduce this risk by supplying relevant external evidence that the model can use to ground its response, although retrieval does not eliminate hallucination by itself.
key_concepts: probabilistic generation can produce unsupported claims
retrieval provides external evidence for grounding
retrieval reduces but does not eliminate hallucination
common_misconceptions: RAG updates model weights
More context always improves quality
Fine-tuning is required whenever documents change

course_reference.section: RAG Fundamentals: Intermediate Q2; RAG Evaluation: separate retrieval and generation evaluation

coverage_enrichment.provenance_note: The local grading guides support likely next-token prediction, confident incorrect continuations, and generation failures despite available evidence. The retrieval risk-reduction wording is a user-supplied synthesis of these ideas.

content: Production RAG systems must manage authorization, freshness, latency, cost, and observability. Metadata filtering can restrict retrieval by tenant or ACL before unauthorized content becomes a candidate. Common failures include wrong chunks, poor ranking, and stale indexes; mitigations include hybrid retrieval, reranking, and synchronized reindexing. Performance and cost should be measured stage by stage across embedding, retrieval, fusion, reranking, context construction, and generation. Production architectures typically separate offline ingestion/index maintenance from online query processing.
common_misconceptions: Prompt instructions alone are sufficient for access control
Optimization should begin without measuring pipeline stages

content: Dense retrieval captures semantic similarity, while sparse lexical retrieval such as BM25 is effective for exact terms, identifiers, acronyms, and rare names. Hybrid retrieval combines their complementary strengths. Reciprocal Rank Fusion combines ranked lists using rank positions rather than incompatible raw score scales. A two-stage pipeline can use efficient first-pass retrieval followed by a more expensive reranker on a smaller candidate set. Retrieval quality must be assessed together with context quality and downstream generation quality.
common_misconceptions: Vector search is always superior to keyword search
Higher recall always guarantees better answers

topic: Defense in Depth and Output Handling
content: LLM input and output should be treated as untrusted at system boundaries. Guardrails should be layered with standard security controls rather than relied on individually. Output passed to downstream tools or systems should be validated and safely handled. High-risk actions benefit from scoped permissions, approval, and monitoring.
common_misconceptions: One guardrail is sufficient protection
LLM output can be executed directly without validation

source.section: Improper Output Handling, Excessive Agency, layered guardrails

content: Prompt injection occurs when untrusted input changes an LLM application's intended behavior. Direct or indirect injected instructions become more dangerous when the model can access sensitive data or invoke tools. Prompt instructions alone are not a complete security boundary.
common_misconceptions: A strong system prompt completely prevents prompt injection

content: Sensitive information should be protected through normal application security controls such as authentication, authorization, least privilege, and data minimization. In RAG, access control should be enforced before unauthorized documents are retrieved into model context; asking the model to respect tenant boundaries is not sufficient.
common_misconceptions: The model prompt is an authorization mechanism

source.section: Sensitive Information Disclosure and Vector/Embedding Weaknesses

content: Agents with tools can create excessive-agency risk when they have unnecessary functionality, permissions, or autonomy. Safer designs minimize enabled tools and permissions, separate read from write capabilities, validate tool arguments, and require approval for consequential or irreversible actions.
common_misconceptions: Agents should receive broad permissions so they can recover autonomously

content: Production AI systems extend beyond a model call. They commonly separate orchestration, knowledge retrieval or tools, model execution, guardrails, and evaluation/observability. Clear boundaries reduce coupling and allow risky actions, data access, and model behavior to be controlled independently.
common_misconceptions: A production AI architecture is only an API endpoint plus an LLM

source.document: OpenAI Practical Guide to Building Agents

content: Production deployment benefits from reproducible runtime environments and separation of configuration from code. Runtime dependencies should be controlled consistently, while environment-specific configuration and secrets should not be hard-coded into source.
common_misconceptions: Secrets should be embedded in source code

content: AI observability should capture enough of the execution path to diagnose failures, including model/tool calls, retrieval or handoff steps, errors, and latency. Tracing is particularly useful for multi-step workflows because final output alone may not reveal the failing stage.
common_misconceptions: Only final generated text needs monitoring

content: Optimization should begin with measurement. Attribute latency and cost to pipeline stages such as retrieval, tools, model calls, context size, and generation, then optimize dominant contributors while measuring quality trade-offs.
common_misconceptions: Optimize the model first without measuring the pipeline

content: Reliable AI applications treat model and tool failures as expected. Timeouts, bounded retries, fallbacks, safe degradation, and escalation should be explicit. Significant changes should be evaluated before broad release and introduced with monitoring and rollback.
common_misconceptions: Retrying forever is a reliability strategy

source.document: OpenAI Practical Guide to Building Agents

content: Scaling requires measuring throughput and concurrency constraints across model/provider limits, network/tool calls, state, retrieval, and application workers. Caching, rate limiting, queues, concurrency, and horizontal scaling can help depending on the bottleneck.
common_misconceptions: Scaling only means selecting a larger model
